summary: Specifies algorithms for wrapping one Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key, and one RC2 key with another RC2 key. Key wrapping lets keys be stored or sent safely. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3217 describes how to protect one symmetric key with another, a job called key wrapping. It gives step-by-step methods for Triple-DES keys and for RC2 keys, using CBC mode with a random starting value. A short checksum stored alongside the encrypted key lets the receiver notice when it has used the wrong key to open it.

subtitle: How one symmetric key is encrypted with another, with a checksum that catches a bad unwrap

tldr.problem: Managing symmetric keys means one symmetric key often has to encrypt another, for example when a shared session key is protected by a key that was agreed with a partner.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives the exact steps for wrapping a Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key, and an RC2 key with another RC2 key, both using CBC mode, a random initialization vector and an 8-octet checksum taken from a SHA-1 digest of the key.
tldr.outcome: The algorithms were republished from section 12.6 of RFC 2630 because they proved useful outside the message syntax they were written for. The checksum gives the unwrapper a way to detect a wrong key, and the security notes insist that the wrapping key be at least as strong as the key it protects.

facts.label: Checksum length
facts.value: 8 octets, taken from a 20 octet SHA-1 digest

today: RFC 3217 is an Informational memo from December 2001 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It republishes the key wrap algorithms that first appeared in section 12.6 of RFC 2630, because they have been found useful in contexts beyond those supported by the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

sections.title: Why a Key Is Wrapped
sections.content:
Management of symmetric cryptographic keys often leads to situations where one symmetric key is used to encrypt, or wrap, another. Key wrap algorithms are commonly used in two situations. First, key agreement algorithms such as Diffie-Hellman generate a pairwise key-encryption key, and a key wrap algorithm is used to encrypt the content-encryption key or a multicast key with that pairwise key-encryption key. Second, a key wrap algorithm is used to encrypt the content-encryption key, a multicast key or a session key with a locally generated storage key-encryption key, or with a key-encryption key that was distributed out of band.

This document specifies the algorithm for wrapping one Triple-DES key with another Triple-DES key, and the algorithm for wrapping one RC2 key with another RC2 key. Both rely on the key checksum algorithm, and both encrypt the content-encryption keys in Cipher Block Chaining mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Two common cases need this: a key that two parties agreed between themselves, and a key kept in storage. In both cases one key protects the other, and the protected key has to be carried or stored in the clear.

sections.title: The Key Checksum
sections.content:
The key checksum algorithm provides a key integrity check value, and it is the same for both key types in this document. The algorithm is: compute a 20 octet SHA-1 message digest on the key that is to be wrapped, then use the most significant, that is the first, eight octets of the digest value as the checksum value.

The checksum is not secret. It travels with the wrapped key and lets the receiver confirm that the key it has just recovered is the key that was wrapped.
sections.plainLanguage: The checksum is the first eight bytes of a SHA-1 hash of the key. It is not secret, and it is what lets the receiver tell a good unwrap from a bad one.

sections.title: Wrapping and Unwrapping a Triple-DES Key
sections.content:
The same key wrap algorithm is used for both Two-key Triple-DES and Three-key Triple-DES keys. When a Two-key Triple-DES key is to be wrapped, a third DES key with the same value as the first DES key is created, so all wrapped Triple-DES keys include three DES keys. However, a Two-key Triple-DES key must not be used to wrap a Three-key Triple-DES key that is comprised of three unique DES keys.

The wrap algorithm sets odd parity for each of the DES key octets of the key to be wrapped, calls the result CEK, and computes an 8 octet checksum on it, called ICV. It concatenates the two into CEKICV, generates 8 random octets as an initialization vector, IV, and encrypts CEKICV in CBC mode with the key-encryption key using that random value as the initialization vector, calling the ciphertext TEMP1. It prepends the IV to TEMP1 to form TEMP2, reverses the order of the octets in TEMP2 so that the most significant octet is swapped with the least significant one and so on, and calls the result TEMP3. Finally it encrypts TEMP3 in CBC mode with the key-encryption key, using an initialization vector of 0x4adda22c79e82105. The ciphertext is 40 octets long.

The note attached to the algorithm is that when the same Triple-DES key is wrapped in different key-encryption keys, a fresh initialization vector must be generated for each invocation of the key wrap algorithm.

The unwrap algorithm runs the steps in reverse. If the wrapped key is not 40 octets, it is an error. The wrapped key is decrypted in CBC mode with an initialization vector of 0x4adda22c79e82105 to give TEMP3, the octets are reversed to give TEMP2, and TEMP2 is split into the IV, which is the first 8 octets, and TEMP1, which is the last 32 octets. TEMP1 is decrypted using the IV as the initialization vector, giving CEKICV, which is split into CEK, the first 24 octets, and ICV, the last 8 octets. The checksum is recomputed over CEK, and if it does not match the decrypted ICV that is an error. The parity of each DES key octet comprising CEK is then checked, and if the parity is incorrect that is an error. CEK is then used as a Triple-DES key.
sections.plainLanguage: The key is padded to a checksum, the checksum is appended, and the whole thing is encrypted twice with different starting values. The second encryption uses a fixed value. Unwrapping undoes both steps and then checks the checksum and the key's parity, so a wrong key is rejected rather than used.

sections.title: Worked Examples from the Memo
sections.content:
The memo gives a full worked example for each algorithm, with the intermediate values in hexadecimal, so an implementer can check a new implementation against a known answer. The Triple-DES example starts from a 24 octet key to be wrapped, a 24 octet key-encryption key, the resulting 8 octet checksum and the random initialization vector, and ends with the 40 octet result. The RC2 example does the same for a 10 octet key, a 16 octet key-encryption key, a length octet, six octets of random padding and the resulting checksum.

sections.title: Wrapping and Unwrapping an RC2 Key
sections.content:
RC2 supports variable length keys. RC2 128-bit keys must be used as key-encryption keys, although the wrapped RC2 key may be of any size.

The RC2 wrap algorithm names the RC2 key CEK and its length in octets LENGTH, which is a single octet, and builds LCEK as LENGTH followed by CEK. It appends padding to LCEK to make LCEKPAD: if the length of LCEK is a multiple of 8 the padding has length zero, and otherwise it contains the fewest number of random octets needed to make the length a multiple of 8. It computes an 8 octet checksum over LCEKPAD, called ICV, appends it, generates 8 random octets as an initialization vector, encrypts the result in CBC mode with the key-encryption key using that random value as the initialization vector to give TEMP1, prepends the IV to make TEMP2, reverses the octets to make TEMP3, and encrypts TEMP3 in CBC mode with an initialization vector of 0x4adda22c79e82105. As with Triple-DES, a fresh initialization vector must be generated for each invocation.

The unwrap algorithm is the reverse. If the wrapped key is not a multiple of 8 octets that is an error. After the two decryptions and the octet reversal, the plaintext is split into LCEKPAD and the trailing 8 octet ICV, the checksum is recomputed and compared, and the result is split into LENGTH, which is the most significant octet, CEK, which is the following LENGTH octets, and PAD, which is whatever octets remain. If the length of PAD is more than 7 octets that is an error, and CEK is then used as an RC2 key.

For protocols that use ASN.1 algorithm identifiers, the RC2 key wrap algorithm has been assigned the identifier id-alg-CMSRC2wrap, and its AlgorithmIdentifier parameter field must be an RC2wrapParameter, which is an RC2ParameterVersion, which is an integer. The RC2 effective key bits, greater than 32 and less than 256, are encoded in that value. For effective key bits of 40, 64 and 128 the values are 160, 120 and 58 respectively, which are not simply the RC2 key length. The value 160 must be encoded as two octets, 00 A0, because the one octet encoding A0 represents a negative number.
sections.plainLanguage: For RC2 the key can be any length, but the key that protects it must be 128 bits. The key's own length is stored as the first byte of the encrypted blob, and the rest is padded with random bytes to a multiple of eight.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect the key-encryption key. Compromise of the key-encryption key may result in the disclosure of all keys that have been wrapped with it, which may lead to the disclosure of all traffic protected with those wrapped keys.

Implementations must randomly generate initialization vectors and padding. The generation of quality random numbers is difficult, and RFC 1750 offers important guidance in this area, while Appendix 3 of FIPS Pub 186 provides one quality PRNG technique.

If the key-encryption key and the wrapped key are associated with different symmetric encryption algorithms, the effective security provided to data encrypted with the wrapped key is determined by the weaker of the two algorithms. If, for example, data is encrypted with 168-bit Triple-DES and that Triple-DES key is wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key, then at most 40 bits of protection is provided: a trivial search to determine the value of the 40-bit RC2 key can recover the Triple-DES key, and then the Triple-DES key can be used to decrypt the content. Implementers must therefore ensure that key-encryption algorithms are as strong or stronger than content-encryption algorithms.

The key wrap algorithms in this document have been reviewed for use with Triple-DES and RC2, and have not been reviewed for use with other encryption algorithms. They make use of CBC mode, and have not been reviewed for use with other cryptographic modes.
sections.plainLanguage: The key that does the wrapping is the crown jewel: if it leaks, every key it has protected leaks too. And a weak wrapping key drags the whole scheme down to its own strength, no matter how strong the key underneath is.
